15481-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers edited this Edinburgh journal number, dated Saturday, February 7, 1852, priced at a penny halfpenny. It opens with Up the Indus, a soldier's plain account of a river journey in India. The writer, a non-commissioned officer of ordnance, traveled from Kurachee toward Roree to join a siege train for Mooltan, ending at Sukkur instead.

He saw some three or four hundred miles of a river unlike others in India, and he tells only what he saw, without books or official sources. That modesty is the piece's charm: a working soldier's view of boats, banks, and towns on the way to war. The number as a whole offers the Chambers mix of travel, fact, and moral reading, made for readers who had little time but wanted the world brought home.
15549-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers edited this Edinburgh journal number, dated Saturday, February 14, 1852, priced at a penny halfpenny. It opens with The Pattern Nation, an essay on France as a country that volunteers experiments in government for mankind's benefit. France tries one form after another, each supposed to be right, then tries something else when it fails.

The essay warns that French projects are not always easy to lay aside, above all in land law. Changing a ministry at the Tuileries does little harm, but meddling with inheritance and the subdivision of lands reshapes property for generations. The number thus offers the Chambers blend: a topical essay, travel, and instruction, written for busy readers who wanted the world explained in short, clear pieces.
16924-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers edited this February 21, 1852 number of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, new series, number 425, priced at a penny halfpenny. It opens with a trip to Venice, leaving Trieste by steamer on a bright September morning in 1851. The writers feared the famous city of the sea might prove overpraised, but they resolved to judge with candor as Alps, Adriatic green, domes, and pinnacles rose from the waves.

Chambers' journal mixes travel, tales, and useful knowledge in a cheap weekly for general readers. The Venice piece shows its plain, observant style, watching a city rise from the sea hour by hour. Readers who love Victorian periodicals will find a pleasant, varied number, best dipped into for its travel and its time.
16953-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-42:
William and Robert Chambers priced this February 28, 1852 journal at a penny and a half for a wide home audience. Its lead piece takes a fresh look at Robespierre, asking whether the feared leader of the French Revolution was truly the monster of common talk. The writer weighs five years of power, the scaffold lists, and the sudden end of the Terror at his fall.

More pieces in the same issue follow the journal's usual mix of history, life, and useful knowledge for plain readers. The Robespierre essay alone makes the number worth a look: it shows mid-Victorian minds testing a dark legend with care. As a whole, the issue is a fine sample of cheap, serious weekly reading in 1852.
28531-the-banner-boy-scouts-snowbound-or:
George A. Warren's The Banner Boy Scouts Snowbound, copyrighted in 1916, sends Stanhope Troop out on skates and iceboats. Paul, Jud, Bobolink, Jack, and their comrades of the Red Fox Patrol won their banner in open competition, and the troop has carried the name Banner Boy Scouts ever since.

Chapters follow the boys on the frozen Bushkill, through an ice-house collapse, a rescue, and an iceboat squadron's tour, into a blizzard, a wild dog pack, and the capture of hobo yeggmen. Warren writes brisk scoutcraft adventure, with first aid, snowdrifts, and forest cabins, for boys who loved the outdoors and the scout code.
366-bab-a-sub-deb:
Mary Roberts Rinehart tells this schoolgirl tale through Barbara Archibald, a sharp-tongued teen who calls herself Bab. Bab writes a school theme on her Christmas break, then keeps a diary of the scrapes that follow. She fumes at being a sub-deb, a girl not yet out in society, while her older sister enjoys full grown-up rank.

Bab schemes, fibs, and lands in trouble with teachers, guests, and a visiting celebrity, yet her voice stays funny and frank. Rinehart lets Bab plead her own case, full of pride and hurt in equal parts. The result is a light portrait of youth on the edge of grown life, eager to be taken as more than a child.
bab-a-sub-deb:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote Bab: A Sub-Deb in 1917, a comic novel told as the diary of Barbara Putnam Archibald, called Bab. A sub-deb is a girl in the year before she comes out in society. Bab chafes at being treated as a child. Her older sister Leila, twenty months ahead of her, is treated as a young lady. Her diary records the injustice in full, capital letters and all.

Bab's schemes run from an invented sweetheart, borrowed to seem grown up, to family rows and school exile. A Christmas holiday full of incidents follows, which she feels bound to report. Rinehart, famous for mysteries, shows her lighter gift here. Behind the fun sits a sharp look at how girls of her class were raised.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agram-zagreb:
Agram, also Zagreb, Latin Zagrabia, is the ancient Croatian kingdom's chief see, in Austria. It was founded toward the eleventh century's end as Kalocsa's suffragan in Hungary, becoming an archdiocese in 1852. Latin Catholics number 1,319,367. There are also 118,304 Greek Orthodox, 9,573 Protestants, 11,929 Jews, and 1,877 Greek Catholics. Agram's 348 parishes have 615 secular and 66 regular priests.

The bishop's city of 20,000 lies pleasantly in a broad plain near the Save, ringed north and west by vine-clad hills. Its monuments are the archbishop's castle-like residence and the medieval Gothic cathedral and sacristy. Three suffragan sees depend on it: Bosnia-Syrmia at Djakovar, Senj, and Krizevac. The people speak Croatian. Agram has a southern Slav university, opened in 1874 chiefly through Bishop Strossmayer's efforts, plus a bishop's seminary, a boys' college, a Greek Catholic seminary, and a school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caleb:
Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite spoke for the tribe of Judah among the spies sent from Cades to scout Canaan. He and Joshua fought the gloomy reports of the other spies and nearly fell to the crowd's fury in the mutiny that followed. For their stand both were spared the decree that condemned the adult generation to die in the desert.

Caleb helped divide the Promised Land among the tribes and, at eighty-five, still in full vigor, claimed Hebron as his portion and took the field to conquer it. He last appears giving his daughter Acsah in marriage to Othniel. A second Caleb, son of Hezron and descendant of Judah, stands apart from him, and the first Caleb likely joined Judah by adoption rather than birth.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-fb:
A short Federal Bureau of Investigation report dated February 2003 sets out a model of the cell that carried out the September 11 hijackings. The bureau drew the model from the lives and acts of the nineteen men. Its aim was to help staff spot a like cell in time.

The report says the men hid in plain sight and kept to Western dress and ways. It traces Mohamed Atta as he sought a fresh passport, asked flight schools for training, and told friends he would study in the United States. One point stands out: at flight school the men sought jet skills such as turns and approaches, not takeoffs and landings. The report treats that narrow aim as a sign worth heeding.

A law enforcement sensitive summary of the PENTTBOM case, dated February 29, 2004, anchors this file from the Federal Bureau of Investigation. PENTTBOM was the bureau's probe into the September 11 attacks. The summary was made for field offices, which were told to send fresh facts to the team at headquarters.

The pages walk through the hijackers' last months in the United States. Sampled text tells of cross-country test flights in August 2001, with men flying out of the Washington area to Las Vegas and Dallas. It notes when men on one flight crew had still not taken their seats in the plot's last phase. Names, dates, and case codes fill the text, and the tone stays that of an internal brief.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: February 2001 gives this file its date in the Federal Bureau of Investigation interview records kept for the September 11 commission work. The pages that survive here are mostly deleted-page sheets. A name, Fahd, can be read in one line, with a note that he advised agents of something he had seen or heard. Past that, the text layer breaks down into codes and marks. The sum is small: an interview record from that month exists, most pages were withheld, and its substance cannot be read from what was freed.

Phone records drive this Federal Bureau of Investigation cable dated February 19, 2002. It went to New York's PENTTBOM team and to bureau posts in six foreign capitals. A warning opens it: phone numbers sent in from abroad had reached the bureau's phone database with gaps, and offices were told of the flaw.

The sampled pages then turn to Hani Hanjour and flight training in Phoenix. The bureau's theory was that he came in June 2001 for time on a flight simulator. Such a device would teach him to take a jet off autopilot and fly it by instruments to its target. Records from the school showed his use of an AST-300 device in April 2001. One page of the log, the cable notes, had been torn out.

A document request from the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks, numbered 23-4 and dated February 2004, forms this Federal Bureau of Investigation file. The commission asked for a copy of security system video said to show Mohamed Atta in Virginia in the first half of 2001. The packet lists videotapes as the item sought. The rest of the file, as freed, is forms and marks too garbled to read. No tape, transcript, or finding is in these pages. The file shows what the commission asked for, not what it got.
frontinus-stratagems-aqueducts-bennett-l:
Charles E. Bennett and Mary B. McElwain translated Frontinus for the Loeb series in 1925. One volume joins the Stratagems and the Aqueducts of Rome together. Frontinus was a Roman general, governor, and water commissioner of the first century.

The Stratagems gather hundreds of military ruses from Greek and Roman history. Generals win by deception, surprise, and psychology in his examples. The Aqueducts then gives his official report on Rome's water supply. The general and the engineer stand side by side in one author. Bennett founded the Loeb Classical Library's Latin series as its editor. The 1925 volume remains the standard English Frontinus for both works.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeShazoJohnWebs: John Webster DeShazo: the illegible handwritten document filed under his name - the OCR is unrecoverable. A ghost in the files, kept as is. Preserved as filed. An obscure item. From the archive's collection, for researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LebherzRichardS:
Richard Lebherz wrote a series for the Frederick Post on Fort Detrick, the Army's biological warfare center in Maryland. The first installment, 'A Deterrent,' ran on November 3, 1969. Its frame was larger than the base itself: Fort Detrick as a symbol of a national crisis over germ warfare.

The series appeared while public argument over chemical and biological weapons was reaching a peak. Lebherz wrote for the base's hometown paper, explaining the work to the neighbors who lived beside it. The first piece sets out the deterrent argument: that germ weapons, like nuclear ones, were held to prevent war by threatening a terrible reply.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Natio: On March 30, 2016, the National Security Archive launched the Cyber Vault, a website built to gather declassified and public documents on cyberspace, cyber conflict, and the governments that wage it. A news post from the Archive announces that launch. The project grew from a simple problem: records of the newest kind of warfare were being classified faster than historians could follow. The posting preserved here is the birth announcement of the collection whose cyber briefs fill neighboring shelves, a small document marking a long effort's start.
